multi-seed/checkpoint averaging, score/rank voting, mixtures of independently fitted
experts, or neural scores combined with separately fitted transition/popularity scores.
Each category must load exactly one independently trained model/checkpoint at prediction.
Jointly trained internal layers/features of one network are allowed. Four category
models are necessary for routing and do not constitute an ensemble. All hypotheses,
code generation, debugging, reviews and memory use must respect this constraint even
if an upstream generic prompt suggests an ensemble. The host audits the actual
predictor before accepting validation scores; violations fail the trial and consume
their training budget. Do not read other trials or reuse their trained checkpoints.

 ## Search results
GRU4Rec’s BPR-max addresses gradient dilution from averaging many easy pairwise negatives. With negative scores r_j, weights w=softmax(r_neg), its regularized objective is −log Σ_j w_j·sigmoid(r_pos−r_j) + λΣ_j w_j·r_j². The logarithm encloses the weighted probability sum; averaging weighted log-sigmoids implements a different loss. High-scoring negatives receive more emphasis without discrete hardest-item selection. [Original paper](https://hidasi.eu/assets/pdf/gru4rec_v2_cikm18.pdf). The official implementation recommends cross-entropy or BPR-max and supports sampling-distribution logQ correction for cross-entropy. [GRU4Rec repository](https://github.com/hidasib/GRU4Rec).

Sampled softmax provides an alternative with implicit hard-negative emphasis; research identifies ranking and popularity-bias benefits, while warning that cosine-normalized representations can limit magnitude learning. These findings motivate comparison, but establish no winner for this Amazon benchmark. [Sampled-softmax study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.02327). False negatives remain a concern: unobserved items can reflect latent interest. UFNRec studies exploiting such samples, although its teacher-based method is unnecessary for the proposed single-model experiment. [UFNRec](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.04116).

Suggested ablation: retain one GRU4Rec model per category; compare regularized BPR-max against sampled softmax using matched negative pools. Then test conservative hard sampling from a larger random pool, retaining random negatives and excluding padding, current positives and observed training-history positives. Treat hardness as informativeness, not proof of irrelevance; temperature smoothing or semi-hard selection are hypotheses for reducing false-negative damage. Never use held-out interactions to filter training negatives. Keep seeds and training limits fixed, selecting exclusively by macro validation HR@10 across all four categories; Electronics separation alone cannot establish improvement.

---

Recent work supports adapting recurrent state updates to distinguish stable preferences from changing intent. [TIEN (2024)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S095741742301905X) incorporates time intervals, item information, hidden states and reset gates into an attention-modified GRU for interest evolution. [FAAM-SR (2026)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0020025526005116) describes a frequency-enhanced GRU that adaptively balances frequent behaviors and exploratory interests. These provide architectural motivation, but neither establishes gains under the pinned RecHarness evaluation.

Direct time-gated GRU precedents predate the requested window. [Sequential Recommender via Time-aware Attentive Memory Network (2020)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.08598) uses a time-aware GRU for short-term intent alongside historical memory; [ACA-GRU (2020)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0020025519308539) modifies update/reset gates using contextual information. A compatible experimental hypothesis is therefore one jointly trained GRU4Rec network whose retention/reset gates depend on the current item, previous state and observed log-scaled time gap. Preserve some state dimensions for persistent interests while allowing others to reset rapidly. This is an inference from the literature, not a verified improvement: compare against the corrected baseline using macro validation HR@10, mask padding updates, read the final nonpadding state, and use only timestamps available consistently during training and prediction.

---

Recent work supports text-derived item representations for sparse-item recommendation, but the retrieved 2023–2026 papers do not establish a directly matching, from-scratch GRU4Rec solution. [TASTE (2023)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.14029) reports improved long-tail recommendations and reduced popularity bias through textual matching, but uses pretrained language models. [CALRec (2024)](https://research.google/pubs/calrec-contrastive-alignment-of-generative-llms-for-sequential-recommendation/) aligns user histories and item descriptions through contrastive objectives, also relying on a pretrained LLM. These provide motivation rather than eligible architectures under the stated constraints.

The closest foundational precedent is [Ask the GRU (2016)](https://arxiv.org/html/1609.02116): jointly learns a GRU text encoder with collaborative recommendation, demonstrating cold-start benefits; also finds supervised mean-pooled word embeddings competitive. Its user model is matrix factorization, so it does not directly validate a sequential GRU backbone. A constraint-compatible hypothesis is to learn randomly initialized token embeddings over titles/descriptions, pool them with a small projection or text GRU, and combine that vector with the item-ID embedding inside one jointly trained GRU4Rec network. Share this item representation between history inputs and candidate scoring, using one recommendation score and checkpoint per category.
